items.p: Kitchen towel held 60 coins and toilet paper held 15 coins. Kitchen towel held ____ times as many coins.
items.why: 60 divided by 15 is 4. Check: 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 60. So the kitchen towel strip held 4 times as many coins.
items.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

chart.title: Strip strength test: coins held by strips 2 cm wide before tearing (made-up middle values)

items.p: Look at the climbing water chart. Which would make the best kitchen towel?
items.why: Water climbed highest up the kitchen towel strip, 9 cm, so it soaks up water fastest. Picking printer paper often means smooth and clean-looking was taken as good. Smooth paper has fewer gaps, so water climbs it slowly.
items.context: This question is about the climbing water test. You hang strips of different papers with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes measure how high the water climbed.

chart.title: Climbing water test: how high the water climbed in 5 minutes (made-up middle values)

items.p: In the stretch test, a band was 8 cm long with no coins, 10 cm with 5 coins and 12 cm with 10 coins. What is the best prediction for 15 coins?
items.why: Each 5 coins added 2 cm. So 15 coins should give 12 + 2 = 14 cm. Picking 20 cm usually means adding the coins to the length, which mixes up coins and centimetres.
items.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang a small bag from a rubber band, add coins five at a time, and measure the band's length with a ruler.

items.p: If you keep adding coins, a rubber band will keep stretching by the same amount for ever.
items.why: False. Every material has an elastic limit. Near it, the band stretches less for each coin, then it snaps at its breaking point.
items.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang a small bag from a rubber band, add coins five at a time, and measure the band's length with a ruler.

items.p: Why does water roll off a lotus leaf in round drops?
opts: The leaf has tiny waxy bumps, so water touches only their tips
Lotus leaves are made of plastic
The water is too cold to soak in
items.why: Tiny bumps covered in wax mean a drop touches almost nothing. Water clings to itself, makes a ball and rolls off. Picking 'hot' is a guess with no evidence. A cold lotus leaf in the morning does the same.

items.p: Why does a packet tear easily at its 'tear here' notch?
opts: The notch is made of weaker plastic
The pull gathers at the sharp tip of the notch, so it tears from there
It is a trick, it doesn't really help
items.why: A notch is a tiny crack on purpose. All the pull crowds at its tip, so the tear starts there. Picking 'weaker plastic' is a sensible guess. But the whole packet is made of the same plastic. Only the shape is different.

items.p: Sort these tests. Does the test break the thing, or leave it whole?
items: adding coins until a strip tears
bending a paper clip until it snaps
bending an aeroplane wing until it snaps
items.why: Tests that leave things whole are called non-destructive tests. They let us check the very thing we are going to use.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: wrote the rule of how springs stretch, in 1678
ran careful fair tests on water's skin in her kitchen
put minerals in order of hardness by scratching, in 1812
a blind scientist who felt that stretched rubber warms up
items.why: All four made careful tests. Two of them, Pockels and Gough, did it with no university lab at all.
items.context: This question is about four people from the history of testing materials.

items.p: A fingernail can scratch chalk. A steel key can scratch the fingernail. Which is hardest?
items.why: A harder material scratches a softer one. The key scratches the nail, and the nail scratches the chalk. So the key is hardest. Picking chalk usually comes from thinking that whatever gets scratched is the strong one.

items.p: Glass is very hard, so it never breaks.
items.why: False. Glass is harder than steel in a scratch test, but it is brittle. It shatters when dropped. Hard and strong are different properties.

items.p: Wet paper tears much more easily than dry paper. Why?
opts: Water slips between the fibres and loosens their grip on each other
items.why: Paper holds together because its fibres grip each other. Water gets between them and weakens that grip. Picking 'water is heavy' is a sensible guess. But a few drops weigh almost nothing, and the paper still goes weak.

items.p: Kabir tested a toilet paper strip 2 cm wide and a kitchen towel strip 4 cm wide. He says kitchen towel is stronger. What is wrong with his test? How would you fix it?
items.a: Two things changed: the paper and the width of the strip. A wider strip may be stronger just because it is wider. I would cut both strips the same size, 2 cm wide and 15 cm long.
items.why: To be fair, only the paper should change.
items.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

items.p: The plastic bag let through 0 ml of water. Does that mean it would make a perfect umbrella? What else would you want to test?
items.a: No. It is waterproof, but an umbrella also needs to be strong, so it doesn't tear in the wind, and maybe light and easy to fold. I would test how many coins a strip of it holds, and whether it tears after folding many times.
items.why: One test checks one property. A real job usually needs several properties.
items.context: This question is about the umbrella test. You stretch a square of material over a cup, pour 25 ml of water on it, and after 1 minute measure how much water came through into the cup.

items.p: Write one sentence of each: what I think, what I saw, and why. Use the climbing water test.
items.a: What I think: kitchen towel soaks up water best. What I saw: water climbed 9 cm up the kitchen towel but only 2 cm up the printer paper. Why: kitchen towel is fluffy, with many tiny gaps between its fibres, so water is pulled up them.
items.why: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good.
items.context: This question is about the climbing water test. You hang strips of different papers with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes measure how high the water climbed.

chart.title: Climbing water test: how high the water climbed in 5 minutes (made-up middle values)

items.p: Draw what you think the edge of a torn kitchen towel looks like under a magnifying glass. Then draw the edge of torn printer paper.
items.a: The kitchen towel edge is fluffy, with loose fibres and big gaps. The printer paper edge is neater, with fibres pressed tightly together and few gaps.
items.why: The gaps between fibres are what let water climb.
items.art: Two empty circles side by side, like two views through a magnifying glass.

items.p: Neel tests a thin rubber band with 10 coins and a thick band with 20 coins. The thick band stretched more. He says thick bands are stretchier. What is the best reply?
opts: He is right, because the thick band stretched more
His test is unfair, because the number of coins changed too
He should have used paper money
Thick bands are always less stretchy, so he made a mistake reading the ruler
items.why: Two things changed: the band and the load. The thick band might have stretched more only because it had twice the coins. Picking 'thick bands are always less stretchy' jumps to a new rule without a fair test. We do not know until we test both with the same coins.
items.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang a small bag from a rubber band, add coins five at a time, and measure the band's length with a ruler.

items.p: Vikram got 9, 2 and 10 cm for the kitchen towel. What should he say the middle value is?
items.why: In order: 2, 9, 10. The middle is 9. The 2 is an odd result, but it cannot pull the middle value far. Picking 7 means working out the average: 21 divided by 3. The average is pulled down a lot by the odd result, which is why the middle value is useful here.
items.context: This question is about the climbing water test. You hang strips of different papers with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes measure how high the water climbed.

items.p: Agnes Pockels's numbers kept jumping about at first. Why?
opts: She was changing several things without noticing, like soap, dust and greasy fingers
She could not read numbers well
items.why: Many small things changed at once. Once she kept everything the same, her results agreed. Picking 'her balance was broken' is a common guess when results look messy. But the balance was the same each time. The surface of the water was not.
items.context: This unit's story is about Agnes Pockels. About 140 years ago, in Germany, she tested the skin of water in her kitchen, by lifting a button off the water with a small balance.

items.p: When you stretch a thick rubber band quickly, it gets slightly warmer.
items.why: True. Stretching lines up its long tangled chains, and that gives out a little heat. John Gough, a blind scientist, noticed this with his lips in 1805.
items.context: In the warm rubber activity, you stretch a thick rubber band quickly and touch it to your forehead.

items.p: Thin glass threads are much stronger, for their size, than thick glass rods. Why?
opts: Thin threads have fewer hidden cracks
Thin threads are made of a different glass
Thick rods are heavier, so they pull themselves apart
items.why: Alan Arnold Griffith showed in 1920 that hidden cracks make materials weak. A thin thread has less room for cracks. Picking 'heavier' is a sensible guess, but a short glass rod is not heavy enough to pull itself apart.

items.p: A paper clip bent once doesn't break. Bent twenty times, it snaps. What is this called?
items.why: Fatigue is when tiny cracks grow a little with every bend, until one snaps. Picking friction is a common mix-up, because the clip gets warm. The warmth comes from bending the metal, not from rubbing.
items.context: In the tap and bend activity, a grown-up bends a paper clip back and forth and counts the bends until it snaps.

items.p: An advert says 'Super Towel soaks up twice as much as other towels!' Plan a fair test to check it. Say what you change, keep the same and measure.
items.a: Change: the towel brand. Keep the same: the size of each sheet, the amount of water, the plate, the time, and the way I squeeze it. Measure: how many millilitres of water each sheet soaks up, by measuring what is left on the plate. Repeat each three times and compare middle values.
items.why: A claim is only as good as the test behind it. A fair test can check it.
items.context: In the kitchen towel project, you test real kitchen towels to see which soaks up most, and which is the best buy.

items.p: Helmets are tested by dropping them, until some crack. Is it right to break things in a test? Give one reason for and one against.
items.a: For: breaking a few helmets in tests means the helmets people wear won't break in an accident. Against: it uses up materials and money, and the broken ones are wasted. Overall, testing things that keep people safe is worth it.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason for each side.

items.p: Which of these can we NOT test directly, so scientists use computer calculations instead?
opts: How strong nuclear pasta inside a neutron star is
How strong a paper strip is
How stretchy a rubber band is
items.why: Nobody can reach a neutron star, so its strength comes from calculations. Picking any other answer misses that we can test those at home today.

items.p: Why do engineers build bridges much stronger than they need to be?
opts: Every piece of material has hidden flaws, and loads can be bigger than expected
Because the law says bridges must be heavy
items.why: Tests show that two pieces of the same material are never exactly the same, and that cracks grow over time. So engineers add a big safety margin. Picking 'cheaper' is wrong: extra strength costs more material and more money.

items.p: Spider silk is about as strong as steel for its thickness, but much lighter and stretchier. Imagine you could make lots of it. What would you make, and how would you test it first?
items.a: For example: a rope for rescuing climbers. I would test strips of it with coins or weights until they break, three times each, and compare with nylon rope of the same thickness.
items.why: A good answer names a use and a fair test that compares it with something we already use.

items.p: Put these in order from softest to hardest, using the scratch test: steel key, chalk, diamond, fingernail.
items.why: Each one scratches the one before it. A fingernail scratches chalk, a key scratches a fingernail, and a diamond scratches a key.
items.context: In a scratch test, a harder material always scratches a softer one, never the other way round. So you can put materials in order of hardness.

items.p: David Kirkaldy carved the words 'Facts not opinions' over the door of his testing works in London. What do you think he meant? Do you agree?
items.a: He meant that what a test shows counts more than what someone believes or says. I agree, but I think opinions are still useful for deciding what to test.
items.why: A thoughtful answer explains the motto and gives a view with a reason.
items.context: David Kirkaldy tested materials for a living in London, from 1866. He built a giant machine for pulling metal bars until they broke.

items.p: Why might Agnes Pockels's work have been nearly forgotten?
opts: She was a woman with no university degree, so few scientists took her seriously at first
She kept it all secret on purpose
Science did not use numbers then
items.why: Her results were careful and correct. Lord Rayleigh saw that, and sent her letter to Nature. Picking 'her results were wrong' is a common guess when someone is less famous. Fame and being right are not the same thing.
items.context: Agnes Pockels did careful tests in her kitchen in Germany in the 1880s. Women were not allowed to study at university there.

items.p: Invent a test for a property we did not test in this unit, like how well a material keeps heat in, or how bendy it is. Say what you would change, keep the same and measure.
items.a: For example: keeping heat in. Change: the material wrapped around a steel cup of warm water, such as wool, foil and newspaper. Keep the same: the amount and starting warmth of the water, the cup and the time. Measure: the warmth of the water after 20 minutes, with a thermometer.
items.why: A good answer has all three parts and a measuring tool.

items.p: Can a test ever be completely fair? Think about the weather, tired hands and tiny flaws in each strip. What can scientists do about this?
items.a: Not completely. There are always tiny differences. Scientists keep as much the same as they can, repeat each test, use the middle value, and tell others exactly how they did it so others can try it too.
items.why: This is a deep question. Good answers notice that repeating and sharing methods make tests trustworthy even when they cannot be perfect.

experiments.title: The Umbrella Test: which material keeps water out?
experiments.question: Which material lets the least water through, so it would make the best umbrella?
experiments.predict: Before you test, put the material squares in a line. Put the one you think will let the least water through first, and the one that will let the most through last. Say why.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the material. Keep everything else the same: the size of the square, the cup, how tight the square is, 25 ml of water, poured in the same way, and 1 minute of waiting. Measure the water that comes through, in millilitres. Test each material three times, with a fresh square and a dry cup each time.

materials.item: squares about 12 cm by 12 cm of: a plastic bag, raincoat cloth or old umbrella cloth, a cotton hanky, newspaper and woollen cloth (3 squares of each)
a steel tumbler or a glass
a rubber band to hold each square tight over the tumbler
a measuring cup or medicine cup with millilitre (ml) marks
a jug of water
a timer or a phone
a tray, to catch spills
a magnifying glass (if you have one)

experiments.safety: Work on a tray and wipe up spills straight away, so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Plan the test and predict. Test each material three times. Fill in the table, find the middle values and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Find the middle value for each material. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each material.

flow.do: 1. Draw three boxes on a sheet of paper. Label them CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME and MEASURE. 2. Fill them in together. CHANGE: the material. KEEP THE SAME: the size of the square, the tumbler, 25 ml of water and 1 minute of waiting. MEASURE: how many millilitres of water come through into the tumbler.
flow.say: Before any test, scientists answer three questions. What will we change? What will we keep the same? What will we measure? Let's fill in our planning boxes.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME, MEASURE. What will you change? What stays the same? What will you measure?
flow.context: This is the first step of the umbrella test. You will find out which material keeps water out best, by pouring water on squares of material stretched over a tumbler.

flow.do: 1. Lay out one square of each material. 2. Ask your child to put them in a line, from 'lets least water through' to 'lets most through'. 3. Write the order down.
flow.say: Which one will make the best umbrella? Put them in a line, best first. Tell me why you chose that order.
flow.kid: Put the squares in a line. Which will keep water out best? Put it first. Say why.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: It is plastic, and water slides off plastic.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the first square tightly over the top of the dry tumbler. 2. Hold it in place with the rubber band. 3. Press the middle down gently, to make a small dip. 4. Measure 25 ml of water in the measuring cup.
flow.say: We stretch it tight, the same way every time. The dip stops the water running off the sides.
flow.kid: Stretch a square over the tumbler. Hold it with a rubber band. Press a small dip in the middle. Measure 25 ml of water.
flow.parent: 25 ml is about 5 teaspoons. Make every square equally tight. A loose square is a change that makes the test unfair.

flow.do: 1. Pour the 25 ml slowly into the dip. 2. Start the timer. 3. After exactly 1 minute, take off the rubber band and lift the square away. 4. Pour the water in the tumbler into the clean measuring cup and read it. 5. Write it in the table. 6. Dry the tumbler. Repeat with a fresh square, three times for each material.
flow.say: Exactly one minute. Now, how much water got through? Read the line on the cup at eye level.
flow.kid: Pour the water into the dip. Wait one minute. Lift the square off. How much water is in the tumbler? Pour it into the measuring cup. Read the line. Write it down.
flow.parent: Ask your child to bend down so their eyes are level with the water when they read the cup. Reading from above gives a wrong number. Water left sitting on top of the square does not count, only what came through.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: 1. Find the middle value for each material. Put its three numbers in order and take the middle one. 2. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each material.
flow.say: For newspaper we got 9, 26 and 24. In order that is 9, 24, 26. The middle value is 24. The 9 is an odd one out. What might have happened in that try?
flow.kid: Put each material's three numbers in order. The middle one is the middle value. Draw a bar for each material.

check.q: In the umbrella test bar chart, which bar shows the best umbrella material?
check.why: The bars show how much water got through. The best umbrella lets the least water through, so its bar is shortest. Picking the tallest bar usually means thinking 'taller is always better'. In this test, a tall bar means a wet head.

chart.title: Umbrella test: water that came through in 1 minute (made-up middle values)

flow.do: Look at the cotton and the plastic through the magnifying glass. Hold each up to a window too.
flow.say: Look closely. Can you see tiny gaps between the threads of the cotton? Can you see any in the plastic?
flow.kid: Look at the cotton through the magnifier. See the tiny gaps? Now look at the plastic. Any gaps?

ask.q: Why did water get through the cotton?
good: It has tiny gaps between its threads.
The water soaked into the threads and went through.

flow.think: The raincoat cloth is cloth, but it kept the water out. What might have been done to it?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the plastic bag would make the best umbrella. What I saw: no water at all came through it, in all three tries. The cotton let through about 20 ml. Why: plastic has no gaps, and water doesn't soak into it. Cotton has tiny gaps between its threads, and water creeps through them.

experiments.context: This is the umbrella test. You stretch squares of different materials over a tumbler, pour the same amount of water on each, and measure how much comes through. The least water through means the best umbrella.

experiments.title: The Strip Strength Test: which paper holds the most?
experiments.question: Which thin paper makes the strongest strip? And what does one tiny cut do to its strength?
experiments.predict: Before you test, feel each paper. Put them in a line, from the one you think will hold most coins to the one that will hold fewest. Then guess: will a strip with a tiny cut hold more, the same or fewer coins?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the paper. Keep everything else the same: every strip 2 cm wide and 15 cm long, taped the same way, the same bag, and only one-rupee coins, placed gently one at a time. Measure how many coins the strip holds before it tears. Test each paper three times. Check every strip for nicks before you start.

materials.item: toilet paper, a paper napkin, a facial tissue and a kitchen towel (enough for 3 strips of each, plus 3 extra kitchen towel strips)
scissors and a ruler
sticky tape
a small plastic bag or paper cup with a string handle
a paper clip, opened into a hook
about 100 one-rupee coins, all of the same kind (borrow from a piggy bank)
a table and a heavy book

experiments.safety: Keep your feet away from under the bag. When the strip tears, the coins fall. A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Cut the strips. Test each paper three times. Test kitchen towel strips with a tiny cut. Fill in the table and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Write the middle value for each paper. Draw a bar chart. Add one more row for the kitchen towel with a cut.

flow.do: 1. Draw three boxes on a sheet of paper. Label them CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME and MEASURE. 2. Fill them in together. CHANGE: the paper. KEEP THE SAME: the size of each strip, how it is taped, the bag, and one-rupee coins added gently one at a time. MEASURE: how many coins the strip holds before it tears.
flow.say: Before any test, scientists answer three questions. What will we change? What will we keep the same? What will we measure? Let's fill in our planning boxes.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME, MEASURE. What will you change? What stays the same? What will you measure?
flow.context: This is the first step of the strip strength test. You will hang a bag from a strip of paper and add coins until the strip tears.

flow.do: 1. Help your child measure and cut strips exactly 2 cm wide and 15 cm long. Mark them with a ruler and pencil first. 2. Cut 3 strips of each paper. 3. Look at every edge for nicks. Throw away any nicked strip.
flow.say: Every strip must be the same size, or the test is not fair. Check the edges. A tiny nick could make a strip tear early.
flow.kid: Measure strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long. Ask a grown-up to help cut. Check each edge for tiny nicks.
flow.parent: Tissue and toilet paper tear while cutting, so go slowly. If your toilet paper is very thin, use two layers for every paper, so it stays fair.

flow.do: 1. Lay the top 3 cm of a strip on the table. Put a heavy book on it, so the strip hangs over the edge. 2. Fold the bottom 2 cm of the strip round the paper clip hook and tape it. 3. Hang the bag on the hook.
flow.say: The book holds the top. The bag hangs from the bottom. Now the strip is doing all the work.
flow.kid: Put the top of the strip under a heavy book. Let it hang over the table edge. Tape a paper clip hook to the bottom. Hang the bag on it.

flow.do: 1. Add one-rupee coins one at a time, placing each gently into the bag. 2. Count out loud. 3. When the strip tears, write down the last number before it tore. 4. Repeat three times for each paper.
flow.say: Gently, one coin at a time. If we drop a coin in hard, it pulls harder than its weight, and the test is not fair.
flow.kid: Place coins in the bag one at a time, gently. Count out loud. When it tears, write down the number. Do each paper three times.

check.q: A toilet paper strip held 14, 15 and 3 coins. What should you do?
options: Use the 3, because it was the last try
Check that strip for a nick, test again, and use the middle value
check.why: The 3 is an odd result. Something probably went wrong, like a hidden nick or a coin dropped hard. Scientists check what happened and test again. The middle value, 14, is not pulled far off by the odd result. Picking 'add them together' gives the total, which is not the same as a result for one strip.

flow.do: 1. Take a fresh kitchen towel strip. 2. Make one tiny cut, about 3 millimetres long, at one edge, halfway down. 3. Test it, three times.
flow.say: Now, the same paper, with one tiny cut. Guess first. Will it hold the same, or fewer?
flow.kid: Make one tiny cut at the edge of a kitchen towel strip. Guess first. Then test it. Did the tiny cut matter?

good: It started at the cut and ran across.

flow.parent: The cut strip usually holds far fewer coins, often less than half. The pull crowds at the sharp tip of the cut. This is why we checked all strips for nicks.

flow.kid: Draw one bar for each paper. Which is strongest? Was your guess right?

experiments.title: The Stretch Test: how far will a rubber band go?
experiments.question: How does a rubber band stretch as we add more weight? Do a thin band and a thick band stretch the same?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If 5 coins stretch a band by 2 cm, how much will 10 coins stretch it? Will a thick band stretch more or less than a thin band, with the same coins?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the rubber band. Keep the same hook, the same bag, the same kind of coin, and measure the same way each time, from the top of the band to the bottom of its loop. Add 5 coins at a time and wait 10 seconds before measuring. Test each band three times.

materials.item: a thin rubber band and a thick rubber band, about the same length (and an old, stretched-out band, if you have one)
a hook, a cup hook or a door handle to hang the band from
a small plastic bag or paper cup with a string handle
a paper clip, opened into a hook
30 one-rupee coins, all of the same kind
a 30 cm ruler, held or taped beside the band

experiments.safety: Never stretch a rubber band towards anyone's face. Stop at 30 coins. Keep your face back from the stretched band in case it snaps.

schedule.what: Hang the bands, add coins 5 at a time, and measure. Draw a line graph and look for the pattern.

experiments.record: Fill in the table of lengths. Draw a line graph for each band: coins along the bottom, length up the side.

flow.do: 1. Draw three boxes on a sheet of paper. Label them CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME and MEASURE. 2. Fill them in together. CHANGE: the rubber band. KEEP THE SAME: the hook, the bag, the kind of coin, how many coins we add each time, and where we measure from. MEASURE: the length of the band, in centimetres.
flow.say: Before any test, scientists answer three questions. What will we change? What will we keep the same? What will we measure? Let's fill in our planning boxes.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME, MEASURE. What will you change? What stays the same? What will you measure?
flow.context: This is the first step of the stretch test. You hang a bag on a rubber band, add coins five at a time, and measure how long the band gets.

flow.do: 1. Hang the thin band from the hook. 2. Hang the bag from the band with the paper clip hook. 3. Hold or tape the ruler beside it, with 0 at the top of the band. 4. Measure the length of the band with the empty bag. Write it down.
flow.say: First we measure the band with no coins. That is our starting length.
flow.kid: Hang the band on the hook. Hang the bag on the band. Put the ruler beside it. How long is the band now? Write it down.
flow.parent: Measure from the top of the band to the bottom of its loop, every time. Changing where you measure from would make the test unfair.

flow.do: 1. Add 5 coins gently. 2. Wait 10 seconds. 3. Measure and write down the length. 4. Keep going, 5 coins at a time, up to 30 coins. 5. Take the coins out and see if the band goes back to its starting length. 6. Do the same with the thick band.
flow.say: Five more coins. Wait ten seconds, because rubber keeps creeping a little. Now measure.
flow.kid: Add 5 coins. Wait 10 seconds. Measure. Write it down. Keep going up to 30 coins. Then do the thick band.

ask.q: Did each 5 coins add the same amount of stretch?
good: At first, yes, about 2 cm each time.
Later it stretched a bit less each time.

check.q: A band was 8 cm with no coins, 10 cm with 5 coins and 12 cm with 10 coins. What is the best guess for 15 coins?
check.why: Each 5 coins added 2 cm. So 15 coins should make it 12 + 2 = 14 cm. Picking 23 cm usually means adding 15 coins to 8 cm, which mixes up coins and centimetres. Picking 13 cm means adding only 1 cm.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a line graph for each band. Coins go along the bottom. Length goes up the side. Join the dots.
flow.say: A line graph shows the pattern. If the dots make a straight line, the band stretches by the same amount every 5 coins.
flow.kid: Draw a dot for each length. Join the dots. Is it a straight line? Where does it bend?

chart.title: Made-up example: the thin band's length as coins are added

flow.think: Robert Hooke found in 1678 that springs stretch in step with the weight. Does your band follow his rule all the way?

flow.do: If you have an old, stretched-out band, test it with 10 coins and compare with the new thin band.
flow.say: This old band has been stretched too many times. Do you think it will be the same as a new one?
flow.kid: Try an old, floppy band with 10 coins. Is it the same as a new band?
flow.parent: Old bands are usually longer to start with and may not spring back fully. They have gone past their elastic limit many times, and sunlight and air slowly damage rubber.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the thin band stretches more than the thick band. Each band stretches in step with the coins at first. What I saw: with 10 coins the thin band was 12 cm and the thick band 10 cm. Each 5 coins added about 2 cm to the thin band, until about 15 coins. Why: the thick band has more rubber chains sharing the pull, so each chain is pulled less.

experiments.context: This is the stretch test. You hang a small bag from a rubber band, add one-rupee coins five at a time, and measure the band's length with a ruler. Then you look for a pattern.

experiments.title: The Climbing Water Test: which material drinks fastest?
experiments.question: Which material soaks up water fastest, so that water climbs highest up it in 5 minutes?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the four materials in order, from the one you think water will climb highest up, to the lowest.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the material. Keep everything else the same: strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long, the same coloured water, each strip dipped exactly 1 cm in, all started at the same moment, and 5 minutes of waiting. Measure how high the colour climbs above the water, in centimetres. Test three strips of each material at once.

materials.item: 3 strips, 2 cm by 15 cm, each of kitchen towel, cotton cloth, newspaper and printer paper
a baking tray or wide dish of water, about 2 cm deep
a pinch of haldi, or a drop of food colouring, to colour the water
a long stick, broom handle or ruler to lay across the tray
clothes pegs or paper clips
a ruler and a timer

experiments.safety: Haldi stains clothes and hands yellow. Wear old clothes and work on newspaper.

schedule.what: Hang 12 strips over coloured water. Wait 5 minutes. Measure, find middle values and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Write the middle value for each material. Draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. Draw three boxes on a sheet of paper. Label them CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME and MEASURE. 2. Fill them in together. CHANGE: the material. KEEP THE SAME: the strip size, the coloured water, how deep each strip dips, the start time and 5 minutes of waiting. MEASURE: how high the colour climbs, in centimetres.
flow.say: Before any test, scientists answer three questions. What will we change? What will we keep the same? What will we measure? Let's fill in our planning boxes.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME, MEASURE. What will you change? What stays the same? What will you measure?
flow.context: This is the first step of the climbing water test. You hang strips of different materials with their ends in coloured water, and see how high the water climbs.

flow.do: 1. Stir the haldi into the water in the tray. 2. Draw a pencil line 1 cm from the bottom of each strip. 3. Peg the 12 strips along the stick, so they hang down. 4. Hold the stick above the tray, ready.
flow.say: The pencil line shows exactly how deep each strip should dip. Same depth for every strip keeps it fair.
flow.kid: Colour the water with haldi. Draw a line 1 cm from the bottom of each strip. Peg all 12 strips on the stick.

flow.do: 1. Lower the stick so every strip dips into the water up to its pencil line. 2. Rest the stick across the tray. 3. Start the timer for 5 minutes. 4. Watch the colour climb.
flow.say: All of them start at the same moment. Watch closely. Which one is winning the race?
flow.kid: Lower all the strips into the water up to their lines. Start the timer. Watch the yellow climb. Which is fastest?

ask.q: What is pulling the water up, against gravity?
good: The water clings to the fibres and climbs the tiny gaps.
The strip is sucking it up.

flow.parent: 'Sucking' is a fine first answer. You can add: water clings to the fibres and to itself, and that pulls it up the narrow gaps. Scientists call this capillary action, or wicking.

flow.do: 1. After 5 minutes, lift the stick out. 2. Lay the strips on newspaper. 3. Measure from the pencil line to the top of the colour on each strip. 4. Write each number in the table and find the middle values.
flow.say: Measure from the pencil line, not from the very bottom. That is where the water started.
flow.kid: Lift the strips out. Measure from the pencil line to the top of the yellow. Write each one down.

check.q: Kitchen towel strips gave 9, 2 and 10 cm. What is the middle value?
check.why: In order: 2, 9, 10. The middle one is 9. The 2 is an odd result, perhaps that strip didn't touch the water properly. Picking 21 means adding them up, which gives a total, not a middle value.

chart.title: Climbing water test: how high the water climbed in 5 minutes (made-up middle values)

flow.do: Tear the end of a kitchen towel strip and a printer paper strip. Look at both torn edges through a magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look at the torn edges. Which one is fluffy, with lots of gaps? Which is pressed flat?
flow.kid: Tear the end of two strips. Look with a magnifier. Which edge is fluffy? Which is flat?
flow.think: A diya wick is made of cotton. Why not printer paper?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: kitchen towel soaks up water fastest. What I saw: in 5 minutes, the water climbed 9 cm up the kitchen towel. It climbed only 2 cm up the printer paper. Why: kitchen towel is fluffy, with lots of fine gaps between its fibres. The water is pulled up the gaps.

experiments.context: This is the climbing water test. You hang strips of four materials with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes you measure how high the water has climbed up each strip.

activities.title: The Planning Board

materials.item: a sheet of paper, a pencil and 8 small slips of paper or sticky notes

schedule.what: Plan a fair test using the three planning boxes and sticky notes.

activities.record: Keep your finished planning board. Use it again for the umbrella test.

flow.do: 1. Draw three big boxes on the paper: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME and MEASURE. 2. Read out the question: 'Which cloth would make the best monsoon bag cover?'
flow.say: Scientists plan before they test. We'll write every thing that could change in a test on its own slip. Then we decide which box each slip goes in.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME, MEASURE. Here is the question. Which cloth makes the best rain cover?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Planning Board. It is a way to plan a fair test before you do it, using three boxes and slips of paper.

flow.do: Write one thing on each of 8 slips. They are: the cloth, the amount of water, the size of the square, the time we wait. Then: the cup, how tight the cloth is, the water that comes through, and who pours. Your child places each slip in a box.
flow.say: Where does each slip go? Remember, only one slip can go in the CHANGE box.
flow.kid: Put each slip in a box. Only ONE slip goes in CHANGE. Only ONE goes in MEASURE. The rest stay the same.

check.q: Which slip belongs in the MEASURE box?
options: The amount of water we pour
check.why: We measure the result: the water that comes through. The cloth is what we change. The water we pour is kept the same. Picking 'the amount of water we pour' is a very common mix-up. One amount of water goes in, the same every time. A different amount comes out, and that is what we measure.

flow.do: Look at the KEEP THE SAME box together. Ask what would happen if one of those slips changed.
flow.say: What if we poured more water on the cotton than on the plastic? Could we still trust the result?
flow.kid: Pick one slip from KEEP THE SAME. What if it changed? Would the test still be fair?

ask.q: What if a different person poured the water each time?
good: They might pour faster or slower.
Better if the same person pours every time.

flow.do: Draw an empty results table below the boxes. The CHANGE slip names the rows. The MEASURE slip names the columns.
flow.say: The table comes straight from the plan. The things we change go down the side. What we measure goes across the top, with its unit.
flow.kid: Draw a table. Write the cloths down the side. Write 'Water through (ml)' across the top. Add Try 1, Try 2, Try 3.
flow.think: Could you plan a test for something at home, like which chappal grips best, or which soap makes most bubbles?

activities.context: This activity is a planning board. Before any test, you sort every possible change into three boxes: what you change, what you keep the same, and what you measure.

setup.caption: 2. Put each slip in a box. Only one slip goes in CHANGE.

activities.title: The One Hair Test

materials.item: one long hair from each family member who agrees, each cut to about 20 cm
sticky tape and a paper clip opened into a hook
a very light paper cup with a thread handle, or a tiny plastic bag
about 40 one-rupee coins, all of the same kind
a ruler and a heavy book

activities.safety: Only use hair that someone has agreed to give. Pull gently. Keep feet away from falling coins.

schedule.what: Test how many coins one hair can hold, for each family member.

activities.record: Make a table: whose hair, coins held on each try, middle value. Write one sentence about what surprised you.

flow.do: 1. Ask family members for one long hair each. 2. Cut each one to 20 cm, using the ruler. 3. Tape the top of the hair under a heavy book at the edge of the table. 4. Tie the bottom of the hair in a tight knot around the paper clip hook. 5. Hang the cup on the hook.
flow.say: One single hair. How many coins do you think it can hold? Guess first.
flow.kid: Take one hair. Cut it to 20 cm. Tape the top under a book. Tie the bottom to a paper clip hook. Hang the cup on it. Guess: how many coins?
flow.context: This is the first step of the One Hair Test. You find out how many one-rupee coins a single hair can hold before it snaps.

flow.do: 1. Add coins one at a time, gently. 2. Count until the hair snaps. 3. Write the number. 4. Repeat with a second and third hair from the same person if they agree. 5. Then test the other family members' hairs the same way.
flow.say: Gently, one at a time. What makes this test fair? Every hair is the same length, tied the same way, with the same coins.
flow.kid: Add coins one at a time. Count until it snaps. Write it down. Test each person's hair the same way.
flow.parent: Many hairs hold between 10 and 25 one-rupee coins, which is roughly 40 to 100 grams. If the hair slips out of the knot instead of snapping, that try is an odd result. Tie it again and repeat.

chart.title: Made-up example results: one hair, 20 cm long

flow.do: Work out how many coins the whole head of hair might hold together.
flow.say: A head has about one hundred thousand hairs. If each holds about 20 coins, together they could hold two million coins. That is about as heavy as two elephants. Of course, the scalp would let go long before that.
flow.kid: Your head has about 100,000 hairs. Together they could hold as much as two elephants! But your head would not like it.

check.q: Why must every hair be cut to the same length for a fair test?
options: So that only the person's hair changes, not the length
Because short hair can't be tied
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Here it is whose hair it is. If the lengths were different too, we could not tell which mattered. Picking 'short hair can't be tied' is a practical worry. But it is not why the test needs the same length.

flow.do: Talk together about what makes hair strong.
flow.say: Hair is made of a material called keratin. Your nails are made of it too, and so are a cow's horns. It is made of long chains twisted together, like a rope.
flow.kid: Hair is made of keratin, like your nails. Inside, it is like a tiny twisted rope.
flow.think: Grandmother's hair and your hair held different amounts. Is that because of age, or something else? How could you find out fairly?

activities.context: This activity tests how strong one single hair is. You hang a little cup of one-rupee coins from a hair and count until it snaps, comparing hairs from your family.

activities.title: The Muffle Test: which material swallows sound?

materials.item: a phone that can play a steady alarm sound, and a second phone with a free sound meter app (or a measuring tape instead)
a large steel bowl or a cardboard box to cover the alarm
covers to test: a towel, a woollen shawl, aluminium foil and two sheets of newspaper
a ruler or measuring tape

activities.safety: Keep the alarm at a gentle volume. Never hold a loud sound close to anyone's ear.

schedule.what: Measure how loud an alarm sounds under different covers, three times each.

activities.record: Fill in a table: cover, three readings, middle value. Draw a bar chart. Put the covers in order from best muffler to worst.

flow.do: 1. Set the alarm phone to ring with a steady sound at a gentle volume. 2. Put it on a table under the upturned bowl. 3. Put the second phone, with the sound meter app, on the table exactly 1 metre away. 4. Measure with nothing over the bowl. Write the number.
flow.say: A sound meter app shows a number for how loud a sound is. The unit is called the decibel. A bigger number means a louder sound. First we measure with no cover at all.
flow.kid: Put the alarm under the bowl. Put the sound meter phone 1 metre away. Read the number. A bigger number means louder.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Muffle Test. You cover a ringing alarm with different materials and measure how loud it still sounds, to find which material swallows sound best.

flow.do: 1. Wrap the bowl in the first cover, one layer. 2. Start the alarm. 3. Read the sound meter after 5 seconds. 4. Write it down. 5. Do this three times for each cover.
flow.say: Same alarm, same volume, same bowl, same distance. Only the cover changes. What else must we keep the same?
flow.kid: Wrap the bowl in one cover. Start the alarm. Read the number. Do each cover three times.
flow.parent: No second phone? Then measure how far away you can walk before you stop hearing the alarm. Use a measuring tape. A shorter distance means a better muffler. Keep the room as quiet as you can, and switch off fans, because noise around you is a change too.

chart.title: Made-up example: how loud the alarm sounded under each cover (middle values)
chart.note: A lower bar means the cover swallowed more sound.

flow.do: Look at the results together and put the covers in order, best muffler first.
flow.say: Which cover swallowed the most sound? Was it the hard, shiny one, or a soft, fluffy one?
flow.kid: Which cover made the alarm quietest? Was it soft and fluffy, or hard and shiny?

check.q: Which kind of material usually swallows sound best?
options: Soft, fluffy materials with lots of air gaps, like wool
check.why: Sound is a shaking that travels through the air. In wool and towels, the shaking gets lost in millions of tiny fibres and air gaps. It turns into a tiny bit of warmth. Hard, smooth foil bounces much of the sound back instead. Picking foil usually comes from thinking a metal wall must block more. Hard walls do block sound well when they are thick and heavy, but thin foil is not.

flow.do: Talk about where people use muffling materials.
flow.say: Recording studios and cinemas cover their walls with soft panels. Why do you think a room with carpets and curtains sounds quieter than an empty room?
flow.kid: Why do cinemas have soft walls? Why does an empty room echo?
flow.think: Hard things ring and soft things hush. Do people have voices like materials? Who in your family is a bell, and who is a blanket?

activities.context: This activity tests which material muffles sound best. You cover a ringing phone alarm with different materials and measure how loud it still is with a sound meter app.

activities.title: The Squash Test: which material springs back?

materials.item: things to squash: a kitchen sponge, a piece of packing foam, a pad of cotton wool, a slice of bread and a folded cloth
a square of cardboard, a little bigger than the sponge
three heavy books, the same three every time
a ruler
a timer

activities.safety: Lower the books gently. Keep fingers out from under them.

schedule.what: Squash five materials under the same books. Measure how thick they are before, during and after.

activities.record: Fill in a table: material, thickness before (cm), thickness under the books (cm), thickness 1 minute after (cm). Circle the ones that sprang back.

flow.do: 1. Stand the ruler upright beside the first material. 2. Measure how thick it is, in centimetres. 3. Write it down.
flow.say: First we measure how thick each thing is, before we squash it.
flow.kid: Stand the ruler beside the sponge. How thick is it? Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Squash Test. You squash different materials under the same heavy books, and measure whether they spring back.

flow.do: 1. Put the cardboard square on top. 2. Gently lower the same three books on top. 3. Measure the thickness now. 4. Lift the books off. 5. Wait 1 minute, then measure again. 6. Do the same for each material.
flow.say: Same books, same cardboard, same minute of waiting. Only the material changes.
flow.kid: Put the card on top. Lower the three books gently. Measure. Lift them off. Wait 1 minute. Measure again.

chart.title: Made-up example results

flow.do: Sort the materials into two groups: sprang back, and stayed squashed.
flow.say: The sponge sprang back. The bread stayed squashed. Scientists call springing back elastic. Staying squashed is called plastic, from an old Greek word that means 'can be shaped'.
flow.kid: Which ones sprang back? Which stayed squashed? Springing back is called elastic.

check.q: The bread was 2.5 cm, then 1 cm under the books, and still 1 cm a minute later. What does that show?
options: Bread is elastic, it springs back
Bread stays squashed: once its air holes collapse, they don't spring back
check.why: The bread did not go back to 2.5 cm, so it stayed squashed. Its walls of soft dough crushed and stuck together. A sponge's walls are springy, so they push back open. Picking 'elastic' means looking at the squash, not at what happened after. Both squashed. Only one sprang back.

flow.think: A sponge, foam and bread are all full of air holes. Why does only one kind spring back? What would happen to a sponge squashed a thousand times?

activities.context: This activity tests how materials squash. You press five materials under the same three books, and measure whether each one springs back to its old thickness.

activities.title: Warm Rubber, Cool Rubber

materials.item: a thick, wide rubber band

activities.safety: Stretch the band away from faces and eyes. Never let it snap. Do not put it in your mouth.

schedule.what: Feel a rubber band warm up when stretched, and cool down when it relaxes.

activities.record: Write: warm, cool or the same, for stretching quickly and for letting go.

flow.do: 1. Hold the thick band against your forehead without stretching it. Notice how it feels. 2. Move it away. Stretch it quickly to about twice its length. 3. Straight away, touch the stretched part to your forehead.
flow.say: Your forehead is good at feeling small changes in warmth. Does the band feel warmer now?
flow.kid: Touch the band to your forehead. Now stretch it quickly. Touch it again straight away. Warmer?
flow.context: This is the first step of Warm Rubber, Cool Rubber. You use your forehead to feel a rubber band warm up when it is stretched.

flow.do: 1. Keep the band stretched for 20 seconds, away from your face, so it cools to the room. 2. Let it go back quickly but safely, holding both ends. 3. Touch it to your forehead straight away.
flow.say: Now the opposite. When it shrinks back, does it feel cooler?
flow.kid: Hold it stretched for 20 seconds. Let it shrink back, holding both ends. Touch your forehead. Cooler?

check.q: A rubber band is stretched quickly. What happens to its warmth?
check.why: Stretching lines up the band's long tangled chains, and that gives out a little heat. When it relaxes, the chains tangle again and take in a little heat, so it feels cooler. Picking 'nothing' is fair if you didn't feel it. Try a thicker band, stretched faster.

flow.do: Tell the story of John Gough.
flow.say: In 1805, John Gough, an English scientist, felt this with his lips. He had been blind since he was a small child. His sense of touch was very sharp, and he found something nobody had noticed. Later, James Joule measured it with a thermometer.
flow.kid: John Gough was blind. He felt this with his lips in 1805. Nobody had noticed it before him!
flow.think: John Gough could not see, so he paid close attention to touch. Can something you can't do make you notice other things better?

activities.context: This activity uses a thick rubber band and your forehead. You feel the band get slightly warm when stretched and slightly cool when it relaxes, as a blind scientist found in 1805.

activities.title: Tap and Bend: testing without and with breaking

materials.item: two steel tumblers, an old cup with a crack (if you have one) and a whole cup, or two clay pots
a steel spoon for tapping
three paper clips of the same kind

activities.safety: A grown-up bends the paper clips. Broken ends are sharp, so wrap them in tape before throwing them away. Tap cups gently.

schedule.what: Tap pots and cups to hear hidden cracks. Count how many bends break a paper clip.

activities.record: Write how a whole cup and a cracked cup sounded. Write the number of bends for each paper clip, and the middle value.

flow.do: 1. Hang each cup from a finger by its handle, or hold each pot gently. 2. Tap it with the spoon. 3. Listen to the ring.
flow.say: Close your eyes and listen. Which one rings clearly? Which one sounds dull or buzzy?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Tap each cup gently with a spoon. Which one rings? Which one buzzes?
flow.context: This is the first step of Tap and Bend. First you test cups and pots by tapping them, which does not harm them. Then you test paper clips by bending them until they break.

flow.do: Talk about who uses the tap test.
flow.say: Potters tap new pots to find cracks. Coconut sellers tap coconuts. Long ago, railway wheel tappers walked along trains at stations, tapping each wheel with a hammer. A dull sound meant a crack.
flow.kid: Potters tap pots. Coconut sellers tap coconuts. Railway workers once tapped train wheels. A dull sound means a crack!

check.q: Why does a cracked cup sound dull when tapped?
options: The crack stops it ringing as one piece
check.why: A whole cup shakes all together and rings clearly. A crack breaks it into parts that shake separately, so the sound dies quickly and buzzes. Picking 'lighter' is a guess. A tiny crack hardly changes the weight at all.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up opens a paper clip into a straight piece. 2. Bend it at its middle, all the way one way and back again. That is one bend. 3. Count bends until it snaps. 4. Do the same with two more clips, bending the same way each time.
flow.say: One bend doesn't break it. Let's count how many it takes. Feel the bend after ten. Is it warm?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to bend the clip back and forth. Count each bend out loud. When does it snap?
flow.parent: Clips often snap after 10 to 30 bends. Each clip gives a different number, which is the point: tiny hidden flaws differ. This weakening is called fatigue. The bend gets warm because bending metal turns some of the movement into heat.

chart.title: Made-up example results: bends until a paper clip snapped

flow.do: Find the middle value of the three clips. Then talk about bridges and aeroplanes.
flow.say: Three clips, three different numbers. That's why engineers can't say exactly when a part will break. So they test many, and they check and replace parts long before.
flow.kid: Each clip broke at a different number. Find the middle one. Engineers check aeroplane parts long before they could break.
flow.think: Which is better for checking a bridge: a test that breaks it, or a test that doesn't? Why do engineers need both?

activities.context: This activity has two kinds of test. Tapping cups and pots checks for cracks without harming them. Bending paper clips until they snap shows how materials weaken after many bends.

projects.title: Our Kitchen Towel Report

materials.item: kitchen towels of two or three different brands (call them Brand A, Brand B and Brand C), or kitchen towel, paper napkins and toilet paper
a measuring cup with millilitre marks
a bowl of water and a plate
a ruler, scissors, sticky tape, a paper clip hook, a small bag and one-rupee coins
the price and the number of sheets of each roll, from the packet

projects.safety: Wipe up spills so nobody slips. A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Test how much water one sheet of each towel soaks up. Test each three times.
Test how strong a wet strip of each towel is, with coins.
Work out the cost of one sheet. Write and share the report card.

projects.record: A report card with a table for each test, the cost per sheet, stars for each towel, and one sentence saying which towel you would buy and why.

flow.do: 1. Look at each packet together. 2. Write each brand's price and number of sheets. 3. Read any claims on the packet aloud, like 'super absorbent'.
flow.say: The packets make claims. Our job is to test them fairly, like a consumer scientist. That is a person who tests things that people buy.
flow.kid: Read the packets. What do they claim? You will test the claims, like a real consumer scientist.
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Kitchen Towel Report, a three-day project. You test real kitchen towels to find which soaks up most, which stays strongest when wet, and which is the best buy.

flow.do: 1. Pour 50 ml of water onto a plate. 2. Lay one whole sheet of Brand A on it for 10 seconds. 3. Lift it by one corner and let it drip back onto the plate for 5 seconds. 4. Pour what is left on the plate into the measuring cup. 5. 50 take away what is left is what the sheet soaked up. 6. Repeat three times for each brand.
flow.say: We pour the same 50 ml every time. Whatever is left behind tells us how much the sheet drank.
flow.kid: Pour 50 ml on a plate. Lay a sheet on it for 10 seconds. Lift it. Let it drip 5 seconds. Measure what is left. 50 take away that is what it drank.
flow.parent: If the sheets are different sizes, cut them all to the same size first, for example 20 cm by 20 cm. Otherwise the test is not fair.

chart.title: Made-up example: how much one sheet soaked up

flow.wait: Day 2: do this step the next day.
flow.do: 1. Cut a strip 2 cm by 15 cm from each brand. 2. Drip exactly 1 teaspoon of water along each strip. 3. Hang it from under a heavy book, like in the strip strength test. 4. Add coins gently until it tears. 5. Repeat three times for each brand.
flow.say: Kitchen towels get wet when we use them. So a fair test of strength should be done wet too.
flow.kid: Cut a strip of each towel. Drip one spoon of water on it. Hang a bag from it. Add coins until it tears. Do each brand three times.

check.q: Why test the kitchen towel strips wet, not dry?
options: Because kitchen towels are used wet, so the test should be like real use
Because wet paper is always stronger
check.why: A good test is like the real job. Kitchen towels are used for wiping spills, so how strong they are when wet matters most. Picking 'wet paper is always stronger' is the opposite of what happens. Water loosens the grip between fibres, so most wet paper is weaker.

flow.wait: Day 3: do this step on the third day.
flow.do: 1. Work out the cost of one sheet: the price divided by the number of sheets. 2. Make a report card, with a table for each test and the cost per sheet. 3. Give each brand 1 to 3 stars for each test.
flow.say: The biggest drinker isn't always the best buy. What if it costs twice as much per sheet?
flow.kid: Work out the cost of one sheet. Price divided by number of sheets. Give each towel stars for each test.

chart.title: Made-up example report card

flow.do: Your child presents the report to the family, and says which towel they would buy and why.
flow.say: Which one would you buy? Is the winner the same if money is tight?
flow.kid: Show your report to your family. Which one would you buy? Why?
flow.think: Brand C was not the best at anything, but it was good at everything and cheap. Is that a kind of best?

projects.context: In this 3-day project, you test real kitchen towels fairly: how much water each sheet soaks up, how strong it is when wet, and how much one sheet costs. Then you write a report card.

challenges.title: Keep the Notebook Dry
challenges.problem: In the monsoon, school bags get soaked and notebooks get ruined. Design a cover for a notebook that keeps it dry when 50 ml of water is poured over it, and still works after it is opened 10 times.
constraints: You may use only one plastic bag, or none.
The cover must open and close, so the notebook can be used.
It must still keep the water out after being opened and closed 10 times.
Test it the fair way: the same 50 ml of water, poured from the same height, for every design.
materials: an old notebook, or a few sheets of paper folded and stapled as a test notebook
newspaper, cloth, wax crayons, a plastic bag, sticky tape, string and leaves
a measuring cup, a tray and a tissue to check for damp
general: Wrap the notebook in plastic, like a raincoat.
Use a zip bag or a plastic sleeve that closes.
Rub wax crayon thickly over paper to make waxed paper.
creative: Make it in layers, like Charles Macintosh's raincoat of 1823: something waterproof between two layers of cloth or paper.
Copy the lotus leaf: a waxy outer surface, so water rolls off.
Copy Kerala's old palm-leaf umbrellas and wrap it in big dried leaves, overlapping like roof tiles so water runs down and off.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own cover. Draw it, make it, open and close it 10 times, then pour the water. Put a dry tissue inside to check. Is it better than the others?

flow.do: 1. Pour 50 ml of water over an uncovered test notebook on a tray. 2. Look at how wet it gets.
flow.say: First, let's see the problem. This is what the monsoon does to a notebook with no cover.
flow.kid: Pour 50 ml of water over a notebook with no cover. How wet does it get?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Keep the Notebook Dry challenge. You design and test a monsoon cover for a notebook.

flow.do: Before making anything, draw two or three ideas and say which property each part needs.
flow.say: Engineers design before they build. Which parts must be waterproof? Which must bend?
flow.kid: Draw two or three ideas first. Which part keeps water out? Which part must bend to open?

flow.do: 1. Make your best design. 2. Open and close it 10 times. 3. Put a dry tissue inside. 4. Pour 50 ml of water over it from the same height. 5. Open it and check the tissue.
flow.say: Opening it ten times is part of the test. Real covers get used, not just looked at.
flow.kid: Make your cover. Open and close it 10 times. Put a tissue inside. Pour the water. Is the tissue dry?

check.q: Your cover kept the tissue dry when new, but after 10 openings the tissue got damp. What does that tell you?
options: The folds or tape got weaker with use, so the test found a real problem
The test was unfair, so ignore it
check.why: Using a cover bends it again and again, like the paper clip. Cracks or gaps can open at the folds. Testing after use found a real weakness. Picking 'ignore it' throws away the most useful result. A good engineer is glad to find a weakness before the monsoon does.

flow.parent: Waxed paper often cracks at the folds after a few openings. Plastic sleeves work well. Layered designs often do best. If every design passes, make the test harder: 100 ml, or 20 openings.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then improve your design once.
flow.say: Here is what designers usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you make yours even better?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ideas and the creative ones. Can you make your cover better? Test it again.
flow.think: People in Kerala made umbrellas from palm leaves long before plastic. What could we use instead of plastic?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a monsoon cover for a notebook, then test it fairly with the same amount of water, after opening and closing it 10 times.

challenges.title: The 100-Coin Strip
challenges.problem: A flat strip of toilet paper 2 cm wide holds only about 15 coins. Using just one sheet of toilet paper and a little tape, make something that holds 100 one-rupee coins.
constraints: You may use only one sheet of toilet paper, about 10 cm by 10 cm, and two small pieces of tape at the ends.
Whatever you make must hang 15 cm from under the book to the hook, the same length as a normal strip.
Add coins the fair way: gently, one at a time.
materials: a heavy book, a paper clip hook and a small bag
general: Fold the sheet into a thick, narrow strip, so there are many layers.
Roll it tightly into a thin tube.
Use the whole sheet, not just a 2 cm strip.
creative: Twist it into a rope. Rope-makers twist jute and coir fibres so they grip each other.
Cut it into three thin strips and plait them, like plaiting hair.
Twist two thin ropes, then twist them around each other the opposite way, as real ropes are made.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Make it, test it fairly, and write how many coins it held. Can you beat 100?

flow.do: Remind your child how many coins a flat 2 cm strip of toilet paper held. Or test one now.
flow.say: A flat strip held about 15 coins. Can the same sheet of paper hold 100, just by changing its shape?
flow.kid: A flat strip held about 15 coins. Can you make one sheet hold 100? Change its shape!
flow.context: This is the first step of the 100-Coin Strip challenge. You change the shape of one sheet of toilet paper to make it strong enough to hold 100 one-rupee coins.

flow.do: List three ideas together before trying any.
flow.say: Before you try, think like an engineer. Write three ideas.
flow.kid: Think first. Write or draw three ideas to make the paper stronger.

flow.do: 1. Make one idea. 2. Hang it 15 cm long. 3. Add coins gently, counting, until it breaks. 4. Try the next idea with a fresh sheet.
flow.say: Same paper, same length, same coins. Only the shape changes. That keeps it a fair test.
flow.kid: Make one idea. Hang it. Add coins until it breaks. Then try your next idea with a new sheet.

check.q: A twisted rope of toilet paper held 90 coins. A flat strip of the same sheet held 15. What made the difference?
options: The shape: twisting packs the fibres so they grip each other
check.why: It is the same paper and the same coins. Only the shape changed. Twisting squeezes the fibres together, so they grip each other and share the pull. Picking 'the paper changed' misses that we used the same kind of sheet. That is what made the test fair.

flow.parent: A twisted rope or a plait usually holds many times more than a flat strip. If 100 coins is too easy, try 200. If the tape at the ends tears first, that is the weakest part of the design, not the paper.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then talk about real ropes.
flow.say: People in India have twisted jute and coir into ropes for thousands of years. Each thin fibre is weak. Twisted together, they can tie up a boat.
flow.kid: Jute and coir ropes are made by twisting weak fibres together. Together, they can hold a boat!
flow.think: Can weak things become strong by holding on to each other? Where else do you see that?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You keep the material the same, one sheet of toilet paper, and change only its shape, to make it hold 100 coins.

opts: Changing only one thing and keeping everything else the same
Testing as many things as possible at once
Doing it as fast as you can
quiz.why: Only then do you know what caused the difference. Picking 'as many things as possible' usually means thinking more testing is always better. If many things change together, you can't tell which one mattered.

quiz.p: In the umbrella test, which of these must stay the same for every material?
opts: The amount of water poured on
quiz.why: The water poured on stays the same. The material is what we change. The water that comes through is what we measure. Picking 'the water that comes through' mixes up what we keep the same with what we measure.
quiz.context: This question is about the umbrella test. You stretch a square of material over a cup, pour 25 ml of water on it, and after 1 minute measure how much water came through into the cup.

quiz.p: Arjun pours 1 spoon of water on cotton and 3 spoons on plastic. What is wrong?
opts: Two things changed: the material and the amount of water
He should have used cold water
quiz.why: With two changes, we can't tell what caused the result. Picking 'nothing' usually means thinking any test that compares materials is fair.

quiz.p: Which tool would you use to measure how much water came through a cloth?
opts: A measuring cup with millilitre marks
quiz.why: Water is measured in millilitres with a measuring cup. A ruler measures length. A clock measures time, which we keep the same. Picking the clock mixes up what we time with what we measure.
quiz.context: This question is about the umbrella test. You stretch a square of material over a cup, pour 25 ml of water on it, and after 1 minute measure how much water came through into the cup.

quiz.p: Which material would you expect to let NO water through?
quiz.why: Plastic has no gaps and water does not soak into it. Picking cotton is a common guess because cotton feels thick. But water creeps through the tiny gaps between its threads.
quiz.context: This question is about the umbrella test. You stretch a square of material over a cup, pour 25 ml of water on it, and after 1 minute measure how much water came through into the cup.

quiz.p: Look at the chart. Which material soaked up water fastest?
quiz.why: Water climbed 9 cm up the kitchen towel, the highest. Picking printer paper often means the smallest number was read as the winner. Here, a taller bar means a faster drinker.
quiz.context: This question is about the climbing water test. You hang strips of different papers with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes measure how high the water climbed.

chart.title: Climbing water test: how high the water climbed in 5 minutes (made-up middle values)

quiz.p: Why should every column heading in a results table have a unit, like (cm)?
opts: So everyone knows what the numbers measure
Because units are always the same
quiz.why: A number like 12 could be 12 cm or 12 coins. The unit tells us. Picking 'to look neat' misses that a table is for others to understand.

quiz.p: Three tries gave 14, 15 and 3 coins. What is the middle value?
quiz.why: In order: 3, 14, 15. The middle is 14. Picking 3 usually means taking the last try. Picking 15 means taking the biggest.
quiz.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

quiz.p: In the tries 14, 15 and 3, the 3 is very different. What do scientists call it?
quiz.why: A result that does not fit with the others is an odd result, or anomaly. Scientists check what went wrong and test again. Picking 'prediction' mixes up what we guess before with what we get after.
quiz.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

quiz.p: A plastic bag let through no water, but it tears easily. What should you do before choosing it for an umbrella?
opts: Nothing, waterproof is all that matters
Test it for strength as well
quiz.why: One test checks one property. An umbrella must also be strong in the wind. Picking 'waterproof is all that matters' forgets that real jobs need several properties. The unit on using materials looks at choosing the right material for each job.

quiz.p: Look at the chart. Which paper would you choose for wiping up a big spill?
quiz.why: Kitchen towel held the most coins, so it is strongest, and it soaks up water fast. Picking toilet paper might come from it being softest. But it tore with the fewest coins.
quiz.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

chart.title: Strip strength test: coins held by strips 2 cm wide before tearing (made-up middle values)

quiz.p: Why does water roll off a lotus leaf?
opts: It is covered in tiny waxy bumps, and water clings to itself instead
The leaf has holes that drain the water
quiz.why: The drop rests on the tips of tiny waxy bumps, so it rolls away. Picking 'holes' is a natural guess. But if water went through holes, the leaf would get wet, and it stays dry.
quiz.context: Raindrops roll off lotus and arbi (colocasia) leaves in round, silver drops, and the leaves stay dry.

quiz.p: A paper strip with a tiny cut held far fewer coins. Why?
opts: The pull gathered at the sharp tip of the cut
The cut made the paper wet
The cut made the strip heavier
quiz.why: At a crack, the pull crowds into the sharp tip, so it tears from there. Picking 'heavier' is not possible, because cutting removes paper. It does not add any.
quiz.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

quiz.p: Inside a rubber band there are long, tangled chains. What happens to them when you stretch it?
opts: They straighten out and line up
quiz.why: Stretching lines up the tangled chains. When you let go, they jiggle back into a tangle. Picking 'they melt' may come from the band getting slightly warm. It warms because the chains line up, not because they melt.
quiz.context: In the warm rubber activity, you stretch a thick rubber band quickly and feel it get slightly warm.

quiz.p: Engineers bent the wings of a new aeroplane until they snapped. Why break a perfectly good wing?
opts: To prove the wings are much stronger than they need to be, so planes are safe
quiz.why: Testing a few things until they break means the ones people fly in will not break. Picking 'faulty' gets it backwards. The test was to show the wings were good.

quiz.p: Can scientists predict exactly how many bends will snap a paper clip?
opts: No. Every clip has its own hidden flaws, so the number changes
quiz.why: Hidden flaws differ from clip to clip, so scientists can only say what usually happens. Picking 'always 10' means one try was taken as a rule. That is why we repeat tests.
quiz.context: In the tap and bend activity, a grown-up bends three paper clips back and forth and counts the bends until each one snaps.

quiz.p: In the muffle test, which cover usually makes the alarm quietest?
quiz.why: Soft, fluffy wool is full of fibres and air gaps, where the sound's shaking gets lost. Thin foil bounces much of the sound back instead. Picking foil is a common guess, because metal seems strong. But strong is not the same as good at swallowing sound.
quiz.context: In the muffle test, you cover a ringing phone alarm with different materials and measure how loud it still sounds.

quiz.p: A sponge springs back after squashing, but bread stays flat. What is springing back called?
quiz.why: A material that goes back to its old shape is elastic, like a rubber band or a sponge. Picking absorbent mixes up two sponge properties. A sponge is absorbent too, but that is about soaking up water, not springing back.
quiz.context: In the squash test, you press materials under the same three heavy books and measure whether they spring back.

applications: Umbrellas, raincoats and school bag covers are made from materials that passed waterproof tests.
Helmets for scooters and motorbikes in India must pass tests and carry the ISI mark of the Bureau of Indian Standards.
Aeroplane wings, bridges and lifts are tested to much more than the biggest load they should ever carry.
Ropes for climbing, fishing and boats are tested until sample pieces break, so the rest can be trusted.
Kitchen towels, nappies and sanitary pads are tested for how much they soak up.
Cricket balls, bats and helmets are tested for hardness and strength.
Doctors test new bone screws and hip joints by bending them millions of times in machines.
Rail engineers check tracks and wheels for hidden cracks using ultrasound.
Potters tap pots, and builders tap tiles, to hear hidden cracks.
Consumer scientists test things people buy, like soaps and towels, to check the claims on the packets.
Packets have 'tear here' notches, which use a crack on purpose.
Self-cleaning paints and windows copy the waxy bumps of the lotus leaf.
Spider silk is tested in labs, so scientists can try to copy it for strong, light ropes and bandages.
New materials for spacecraft are tested outside the International Space Station, in the cold, heat and radiation of space.

open_questions.q: Can we ever predict exactly when a material will break?
open_questions.why_open: Every piece has its own hidden flaws, too small to see. Scientists can say what usually happens, but not exactly what one piece will do.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does the very first crack start inside a metal that is bent again and again?
open_questions.why_open: It starts with rows of atoms slipping, deep inside. Scientists study it with powerful microscopes and computers, and still argue about the details.

open_questions.q: How do spiders make silk so strong, from a liquid, at room temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand parts of it. But nobody has yet made silk as good as a spider's, in large amounts.

open_questions.q: Is there a strongest possible material?
open_questions.why_open: New materials keep breaking records. Calculations suggest nuclear pasta in neutron stars may be strongest of all, but nobody can test it.

open_questions.q: How can we test materials that must last hundreds of years, like the walls of a nuclear waste store?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can wait hundreds of years. Scientists speed up tests with heat and stress, and argue about whether fast tests really match slow time.

open_questions.q: How long does plastic really last in sun, soil and sea?
open_questions.why_open: Most plastics have only existed for about 70 years. The very long numbers you hear are estimates, still being tested.

open_questions.q: Why do some tests give different answers in different labs?
open_questions.why_open: Tiny differences in materials, tools and people's methods can change results. Scientists are still finding the best ways to make tests repeatable everywhere.
