Why do we try things three times, not just once?
Which of your clothes would pass the umbrella test? Which would fail?
Why does the milk packet tear so easily at the notch?
How could you find out which of your pens writes the longest line before running out, fairly?
The potter tapped the pot. What was she listening for?
Is it fair to test everyone in a class with the same test? Why or why not?
If one hair can hold 20 coins, what could a plait of three hairs hold? How could you check?
Did anything today give an odd result? What might have gone wrong?

maths.problem: A toilet paper strip was tested three times. It held 14 coins, then 15 coins, then 3 coins. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the three numbers in order, from smallest to biggest: 3, 14, 15. The one in the middle is 14. So the middle value is 14 coins. The 3 is an odd result, but it does not change the middle value much. If we added them all up and shared by 3, we would get only about 11, because the odd result pulls it down.
maths.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

answer_chart.title: Three tries with a toilet paper strip

maths.why_maths: Three tries give three numbers, but we need one number for each paper. Putting them in order and taking the middle one gives a fair single result that one fluke cannot spoil.

maths.problem: In the umbrella test, these are the middle values for water that came through: plastic bag 0 ml, raincoat cloth 1 ml, cotton hanky 20 ml, newspaper 24 ml. Draw a bar chart. Which material would make the worst umbrella?
maths.answer: Newspaper would make the worst umbrella. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each material, as tall as its number. The tallest bar is newspaper, at 24 ml. In this test, the tallest bar means the most water got through. So newspaper is the worst umbrella, and the plastic bag, with no bar at all, is the best.
maths.context: This question is about the umbrella test. You stretch a square of material over a cup, pour 25 ml of water on it, and after 1 minute measure how much water came through into the cup.

answer_chart.title: Umbrella test: water that came through in 1 minute (made-up middle values)

maths.why_maths: A list of numbers is hard to compare at a glance. A bar chart turns them into bars, so the best and worst materials jump out.

maths.problem: Asha measured her rubber band's stretch in finger-widths: 5 finger-widths. Her father measured the same band and got 3 finger-widths. Then they both used a ruler, and both got 8 cm. Why did the ruler agree, when the fingers did not?
maths.answer: Because a centimetre is the same size for everyone, but fingers are not.
maths.explain: Asha's fingers are thinner than her father's, so the same stretch takes more of her finger-widths. A centimetre is a standard unit. It is exactly the same size on every ruler in the world. So both of them got 8 cm.
maths.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang a small bag from a rubber band, add coins five at a time, and measure the band's length with a ruler.
maths.why_maths: Tests are only useful if other people can repeat them and compare. Standard units like the centimetre let everyone measure the same way.

maths.problem: A rubber band was 8 cm long with no coins. With 5 coins it was 10 cm. With 10 coins it was 12 cm. If the pattern keeps going, how long will it be with 15 coins? And with 20 coins?
maths.answer: 14 cm with 15 coins, and 16 cm with 20 coins, if the pattern keeps going.
maths.explain: Every 5 coins add 2 cm. 12 + 2 = 14 cm for 15 coins. 14 + 2 = 16 cm for 20 coins. But real bands stop following the pattern near their limit. In the made-up results, the band was only 15 cm at 20 coins. A pattern is a prediction, and a test checks it.
maths.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang a small bag from a rubber band, add coins five at a time, and measure the band's length with a ruler.

answer_chart.title: The rubber band pattern: predicted and measured

maths.why_maths: Spotting a number pattern lets you predict the next result before you test it. Then the test tells you if the pattern really holds.

maths.problem: Brand A kitchen towel costs 120 rupees for 60 sheets. Brand C costs 60 rupees for 60 sheets. How much does one sheet of each cost? Which is the better buy, if both soak up about the same?
maths.answer: Brand A costs 2 rupees a sheet. Brand C costs 1 rupee a sheet. Brand C is the better buy.
maths.explain: To find the cost of one sheet, share the price by the number of sheets. 120 divided by 60 is 2, so Brand A is 2 rupees a sheet. 60 divided by 60 is 1, so Brand C is 1 rupee a sheet. If they soak up about the same, Brand C gives the same job for half the money.
maths.context: This is about Our Kitchen Towel Report project. You test kitchen towels fairly, then work out how much one sheet of each costs.
maths.why_maths: A test tells you which towel works best. Dividing the price by the number of sheets tells you which one gives the most for your money.

maths.problem: Look at the measuring cup in the picture. The big numbers go up in 10s of millilitres. Each small mark is 2 millilitres. How much water came through the cotton?
maths.explain: The water is past the 20 line. It reaches the first small mark above 20. Each small mark is 2 millilitres. So it is 20 + 2 = 22 millilitres.
maths.context: This question is about the umbrella test. You stretch a square of material over a cup, pour 25 ml of water on it, and after 1 minute measure how much water came through into the cup.

roots.context: We have been testing materials: pulling, soaking, stretching and squashing them to find out what they really are. Now we ask what testing tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: We only know what we test. And every test is asked by someone.
deep_truth.habit: We think facts just sit there. But a result depends on the question, the test and who did it. Change one thing at a time, and the world answers honestly.
deep_truth.evidence: Changing two things at once gives an answer nobody can trust.

three.who_am_i: You are made of materials too. One of your hairs held about 20 coins, and your bones mend their own cracks.
three.what_is_life: Life is full of tests. A test is not a punishment. It is a way of finding out what is true.
three.what_is_this_world: Every material, from tissue to steel to a far-off star, is the same tiny atoms holding on to each other in different ways.

roots.thread: Paper, rubber, wool and steel look like completely different things. Zoom in far enough, and each one is made of atoms, held together by the same electric pull. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as the many: one kind of stuff, holding on in countless different ways. When we test a material, it shows us how it holds on: it bends, or springs back, or snaps. A fair test is a way of letting each thing speak for itself.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha told the people of Kesaputta, called the Kalamas, not to believe something only because it is old, or written down, or said by a respected teacher. When you know for yourselves, by looking carefully, that something is good and true, then accept it.
teachings.link: This is the spirit of a fair test. We do not believe the advert or the shopkeeper. We test, and let the results decide.

teachings.teaching: When people are alive, they are soft and bendy. When they die, they become hard and stiff. Green plants are soft and supple. Dry ones are brittle. So the stiff and hard break, and the soft and bending last.
teachings.link: Our tests showed this too. Glass is hard but shatters. Rubber and bamboo bend and spring back. A twisted rope of soft fibres held far more than a flat strip.

teachings.teaching: Krishna says that the true self cannot be cut by weapons, burned by fire, wetted by water or dried by the wind.
teachings.link: These are almost exactly our tests: cutting, soaking, drying and heating. Every material we tested had a breaking point. The Gita asks whether there is something in us that has none.

science.text: Every material, from tissue paper to steel, holds together by the same kind of force: electric pulls between its atoms.
Nobody can yet predict the exact moment one particular piece of material will break. Each piece has its own hidden flaws.

other_view.who: The Charvaka thinkers of ancient India, and many scientists today
other_view.view: The Charvaka school taught that only what we can perceive is real. Many scientists today would say a material is just atoms and forces, and a test is just a measurement. In this view there is no One behind the many, and nothing in us is beyond every test. These are honest views, and many careful people hold them.

practice.title: Stiff Like Glass, Soft Like Bamboo
practice.say: Stand up. First, make your whole body stiff, like a glass rod. Lock your knees, clench your hands and hold your breath for three seconds. Now let it all go. Breathe out slowly. Now be a bamboo in the wind. Let your arms and body sway gently. Breathe in for four counts and out for four counts, five times. Then stand still and notice. How does your body feel now? Which felt stronger: stiff or swaying?
practice.kid: Stand up. Make your body stiff as glass. Hold your breath for three seconds. Now let go. Sway like bamboo in the wind. Breathe in for four, out for four, five times. Stand still. How do you feel?

ask: When something hard happens to you, are you more like glass, rubber or bamboo?
Is there anything in you that no test could ever cut, burn or wet?
